Scope and authority
This is a compliance-engineer reading of DOE 10 CFR Part 431, Subpart K, §431.196, as in force on 2026-11-21. The operative source text is the paragraph language introducing each table in §431.196(a)(2) and §431.196(b)(2), not the kVA/efficiency rows of the tables.

Answer
1. §431.196(a)(2) — Low-Voltage Dry-Type Distribution Transformers
The stated manufacture-date window is:

  'manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029'

Calendar-date equivalent: manufacture dates from 2016-01-01 through 2029-04-22 inclusive. The start date is inclusive; the end date is exclusive at 2029-04-23.

This window applies to the table referenced by (a)(2) for all kVA ratings and both single-phase and three-phase columns. The table rows themselves state only kVA and efficiency values; they do not contain separate row-by-row manufacture-date windows.

2. §431.196(b)(2) — Liquid-Immersed Distribution Transformers
The stated manufacture-date window is the same:

  'manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029'

Calendar-date equivalent: manufacture dates from 2016-01-01 through 2029-04-22 inclusive. The start date is inclusive; the end date is exclusive at 2029-04-23.

This window applies to the table referenced by (b)(2) for all kVA ratings and both single-phase and three-phase columns. As with (a)(2), the table rows state only kVA and efficiency values, not separate date windows.

Key boundary and transition
- The preceding window in §431.196(a)(1) and (b)(1) is 'manufactured on or after January 1, 2007, but before January 1, 2016'.
- The next window begins on or after April 23, 2029. For low-voltage dry-type transformers this is §431.196(a)(3). For liquid-immersed transformers the post-2029 tiers include §431.196(b)(3), with submersible transformers addressed separately in §431.196(b)(4).
- Therefore, for the precise date 2029-04-22, the (a)(2)/(b)(2) tables apply; for 2029-04-23 and later, the next-tier tables apply.

Table caption note
In the published text, the table following §431.196(a)(2) carries the caption 'Table 2 to Paragraph (a)(1)' in the source. That is an apparent caption/labeling artifact. The paragraph (a)(2) text expressly introduces the 'following table' and states the 2016-01-01 to 2029-04-22 window. The caption does not alter the manufacture-date window.

Definitions confirming the equipment classes
- 'Low-voltage dry-type distribution transformer' means a distribution transformer with an input voltage of 600 volts or less whose core and coil assembly is immersed in a gaseous or dry-compound insulating medium.
- 'Liquid-immersed distribution transformer' means a distribution transformer in which the core and coil assembly is immersed in an insulating liquid.

Compliance application
A transformer falls in the §431.196(a)(2) or §431.196(b)(2) window if its date of manufacture is on or after 2016-01-01 and before 2029-04-23. Do not apply the 2007-01-01 to 2015-12-31 window from paragraph (a)(1)/(b)(1), and do not apply the on-or-after-2029-04-23 window to equipment manufactured before that date.

verdict.summary:
WRITTEN INFORMATION REQUIRED FROM A DISTRIBUTOR ON REQUEST — Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002 (S.I. 2002 No. 2665), original (as made) text

1. SOURCE AND VERSION CONTROL (satisfying the 'original as made' constraint)

Instrument: The Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002, S.I. 2002 No. 2665. Made 24 October 2002; laid before Parliament 28 October 2002; coming into force 31 January 2003. Made by the Secretary of State under sections 29, 30(3) and 60 of the Electricity Act 1989; signed Brian Wilson, Minister of State for Energy and Construction, DTI, 24 October 2002.

Version authority relied on: the legislation.gov.uk 'Original (As made)' view of the instrument, which is annotated 'Status: This is the original version (as it was originally made)' and 'The original version of the legislation as it stood when it was enacted or made. No changes have been applied to the text', cross-checked against the 'Original Print PDF of King's Printer Version' (uksi_20022665_en.pdf), described as 'the original PDF of the as made version that was used to publish the official printed copy', which 'does not include any changes made by correction slips'. The 'More Resources' page records no correction slips and 'There are no associated documents for this legislation.'

Conclusion on version: the operative words of regulation 28 in the as-made print PDF and in the current legislation.gov.uk text are identical for items (a)–(e); the only differences are editorial (extent markers 'E+W+S' and spacing). Therefore the provision is unamuted in substance, and the answer below is valid for the original as-made version as required.

2. THE GOVERNING PROVISION — regulation 28, as made (verbatim)

'Information to be provided on request
28. A distributor shall provide, in respect of any existing or proposed consumer's installation which is connected or is to be connected to his network, to any person who can show a reasonable cause for requiring the information, a written statement of—
(a) the maximum prospective short circuit current at the supply terminals;
(b) for low voltage connections, the maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation;
(c) the type and rating of the distributor's protective device or devices nearest to the supply terminals;
(d) the type of earthing system applicable to the connection; and
(e) the information specified in regulation 27(1),
which apply, or will apply, to that installation.'

3. ANSWER — THE WRITTEN INFORMATION REQUIRED, TOPIC BY TOPIC

The four topics named in the request correspond exactly to regulation 28(a)–(d). The distributor must provide a WRITTEN STATEMENT of the following, being the matters that 'apply, or will apply, to that installation':

(1) Supply terminals — regulation 28(a): the maximum prospective short circuit current at the supply terminals.

(2) Earth fault path — regulation 28(b): for low voltage connections, the maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation. (Note the two built-in limits: the item is expressed only 'for low voltage connections', and the impedance stated is that of the earth fault path OUTSIDE the installation — i.e. the distributor's portion of the loop — not the whole loop.)

(3) Nearest protective devices — regulation 28(c): the type and rating of the distributor's protective device or devices nearest to the supply terminals. (Both 'type' AND 'rating' are required; singular 'device' or plural 'devices' is covered.)

(4) Earthing system — regulation 28(d): the type of earthing system applicable to the connection.

Scope-adjacent mandatory item (outside the four topics asked): regulation 28(e) additionally requires the written statement to include 'the information specified in regulation 27(1)' — i.e. the distributor's declared supply characteristics under regulation 27. It is part of the same written statement but is not one of the four topics in the request.

4. WHO MAY REQUIRE THE INFORMATION

The duty is owed to 'any person who can show a reasonable cause for requiring the information'. It is NOT confined to the consumer: a third party (for example, an electrical contractor, consulting engineer or prospective purchaser) who can show reasonable cause may demand it. 'Reasonable cause' is the only gate; the regulation does not define it or prescribe how it is shown.

5. INSTALLATION SCOPE

The statement is given 'in respect of any existing or proposed consumer's installation which is connected or is to be connected to his network'. Both existing and proposed connections are covered. The qualifying words at the end — 'which apply, or will apply, to that installation' — make the statement installation-specific: the figures and descriptions must be those applicable (or prospectively applicable) to that particular installation, not generic network data. For a proposed connection, forward-looking ('will apply') values must be given.

6. FORM, TIMING, AND EXCEPTIONS

Form: a 'written statement' is required — oral provision does not discharge the duty.
Timing: regulation 28 as made fixes no deadline, no fee, and no prescribed format; those matters are not dealt with by the regulation itself.
Exceptions/qualifications: regulation 28 contains NO safety, confidentiality, commercial-in-confidence, or 'unreasonable' carve-out, and no 'so far as reasonably practicable' hedge. This is significant by contrast with other provisions of the same instrument, e.g. regulation 24(4) ('Unless he can reasonably conclude that it is inappropriate for reasons of safety, a distributor shall...'), and regulations 6 and 8 ('so far as is reasonably practicable'). Where the draftsman intended a qualification he used one; regulation 28's duty, once reasonable cause is shown, is unqualified as to content and form.

7. AMENDED/CURRENT VERSION COMPARISON

No material difference for these items. The as-made print PDF and the current text of regulation 28(a)–(e) are word for word identical. Differences between renderings are limited to editorial extent annotations ('E+W+S') and typographical spacing. Any later amendment affecting other parts of the Regulations does not alter the item list at issue here.

8. CONSOLIDATED ANSWER

Under regulation 28 of the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002 (S.I. 2002/2665) as originally made, a distributor must, on request by any person who can show a reasonable cause for requiring the information and in respect of any existing or proposed consumer's installation connected or to be connected to the distributor's network, provide a written statement of: (a) the maximum prospective short circuit current at the supply terminals; (b) for low voltage connections, the maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation; (c) the type and rating of the distributor's protective device or devices nearest to the supply terminals; and (d) the type of earthing system applicable to the connection — together with (e) the information specified in regulation 27(1) — each item being that which applies, or will apply, to that installation.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Minimum rated working pressure required for valves, fittings, and accessories connected directly to an LP-Gas container, including primary shutoff valves, under 29 CFR 1910.110 as in force on 2026-11-21: 250 psig (pounds per square inch gauge; approximately 1.72 MPa gauge).

This is a floor, not a target. Every such component must be rated at or above 250 psig; a component marked 250 psig WOG/250 psig LP-Gas meets the rule, anything rated below it does not.


1. OPERATIVE REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim)

29 CFR 1910.110, subparagraph '(7) Container valves and container accessories', item (i):

  '(i) Valves, fittings, and accessories connected directly to the container including primary shutoff valves, shall have a rated working pressure of at least 250 p.s.i.g. and shall be of material and design suitable for LP-Gas service. Cast iron shall not be used for container valves, fittings, and accessories. This does not prohibit the use of container valves made of malleable or nodular iron.'

This is the provision that answers the question exactly as phrased ('connected directly to the container including primary shutoff valves').


2. CITATION AND VERSION VERIFICATION (constraint: as in force 2026-11-21)

- 29 CFR 1910.110, 'Container valves and container accessories', item (7)(i). Quote above is verbatim from the fetched text.
- Same 250 psig floor, independently stated, in the companion subparagraph '(5) Valves and accessories':
    (5)(i): 'Container valves and accessories shall have a rated working pressure of at least 250 p.s.i.g., and shall be of a type suitable for liquefied petroleum gas service.'
    (5)(vi): 'Fittings shall be steel, malleable iron, or brass having a minimum working pressure of 250 p.s.i.g. Cast iron pipe fittings, such as ells, tees, and unions shall not be used.'
- Version control: the text was retrieved from (a) eCFR 'current' Title 29, Subtitle B, Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart H, Sec. 1910.110 (captured 2026-11-23T10:46:41Z, sha256 f87fb8ebd6aa), (b) the GPO 2025 annual edition, title 29 volume 5, XML and PDF (sha256 8afa22fd6db0 / 7591b76f956e). The three agree word-for-word on (7)(i). No amendment affecting this paragraph is evidenced between the 2025 annual edition and the capture date, so the requirement in force on 2026-11-21 is 250 psig.
- Caveat on the capture date: eCFR 'current' was snapshotted two days AFTER the target date. If an amendment had taken effect on 2026-11-22 or 2026-11-23, the snapshot would not represent 2026-11-21. Because the 2025 print edition matches the snapshot exactly, no such change is indicated; before filing a formal compliance document, confirm via eCFR's 'Changes to 1910.110' / Federal Register history that no document affecting (7)(i) took effect in that two-day window.
- Citation-precision caveat: the retrieved excerpt preserves the numbered subparagraph headings '(5)' and '(7)' but not the top-level lettered designation, and the section's internal cross-references ('paragraph (b)(5)(iii)', 'paragraph (e)(5)(iv)(c)') show the lettered path is not self-evident. Cite as 29 CFR 1910.110, 'Container valves and container accessories' (7)(i), quote the text verbatim, and confirm the full alphanumeric anchor in eCFR's paragraph links before pasting into a formal document. The numeric requirement (250 psig) is not affected by which letter prefixes the paragraph.


3. CORROBORATING 250 PSIG PROVISIONS IN THE SAME SECTION

Every related pressure figure in 1910.110 is the same 250 psig, which is why the answer is not ambiguous:

  Provision                                                    Requirement
  (7)(i) Container valves/fittings/accessories, direct          >= 250 psig rated working pressure
  (5)(i) Container valves and accessories                        >= 250 psig rated working pressure
  (5)(vi) Fittings (steel, malleable iron, or brass)             >= 250 psig minimum working pressure
  (10) Pump accessories                                          >= 250 psig rated working pressure
  (11)(i) Dispensing devices: meters, vapor separators,          >= 250 psig minimum working pressure
          valves and fittings in the dispenser
  Lettered container-connection block (c): manifolds and         >= 250 psig service pressure
          fittings from container to regulator inlet
  Lettered container-connection block (g)(1): hose and           >= 250 psig working pressure
          hose connections
  Lettered block (iv): all shutoff valves (liquid or gas);       >= 250 psig rated working pressure where
          valves subject to container pressure                    subject to container pressure


4. SCOPE DETERMINATION

- Liquid and vapor service: (7)(i) draws no liquid/vapor distinction. The 250 psig floor applies to both. The liquid/vapor distinction appears elsewhere (e.g., excess-flow valve sizing, main shutoff valves on liquid and vapor lines must be readily accessible) and does not relax the pressure rating.
- 'Connected directly to the container': components at the container connection itself, including the primary (main) shutoff valve, the container service valve, the filler connection hardware, container-mounted regulators and the manifold/fittings feeding a regulator inlet, and container-mounted gaging/accessory hardware. Downstream piping beyond the container connection is governed by the piping provisions rather than (7)(i), but the 250 psig figure recurs for hose, dispensing devices, and pump accessories, so there is no place in the section where a lower rating is permitted for LP-Gas wetted hardware.
- Materials restrictions that ride along with the pressure rating (all in the same paragraph and worth capturing in the purchase spec): cast iron shall not be used for container valves, fittings, and accessories; container valves of malleable or nodular iron are permitted; fittings shall be steel, malleable iron, or brass; cast iron pipe fittings (ells, tees, unions) are prohibited; valve seats, packing, gaskets, and diaphragms must be resistant to LP-Gas.
- Related siting rule to design around: (7)(ii) requires shutoff valves on container connections to be located as close to the container as practicable (exceptions: safety relief connections, liquid level gaging devices, plugged openings).


5. APPLICATION: BOM / DESIGN-REVIEW CHECKLIST

Use this as the acceptance test for a bill of materials or a layout review:

  [ ] Every valve, fitting, and accessory at the container connection carries a marked or published rated working pressure >= 250 psig. Record the number and the source document (catalog page, nameplate photo, or data sheet revision) per line item.
  [ ] Primary shutoff valve is included in that set (not exempt) and is located as close to the container as practicable.
  [ ] No cast iron anywhere in container valves, fittings, or accessories. Malleable/nodular iron only where the item is a container valve.
  [ ] Fittings are steel, malleable iron, or brass. No cast iron ells, tees, or unions.
  [ ] Elastomers (seats, packing, gaskets, diaphragms, hose liner) are LP-Gas resistant and rated for the same pressure class as the body.
  [ ] Hose and hose connections >= 250 psig working pressure; hose assemblies not re-used after end-fitting swage or field repair unless the assembly is re-rated.
  [ ] Manifold and fittings from container to regulator inlet >= 250 psig service pressure.
  [ ] Container marking per the section's marking provision is present and legible after coating/painting.
  [ ] Assembled piping leak-tested after assembly at not less than normal operating pressure (per the section's piping test item); document test medium, pressure, duration, and leak-detection method.

Suggested purchase-spec language: 'All valves, fittings, and accessories furnished for direct connection to the LP-Gas container, including the primary shutoff valve, shall have a published rated working pressure of not less than 250 psig (1.72 MPa gauge), shall be of material and design suitable for LP-Gas service, and shall contain no cast iron pressure-retaining parts. Fittings shall be steel, malleable iron, or brass. Elastomers shall be resistant to LP-Gas. Certified data sheets showing the rated working pressure shall accompany the submittal.'


6. DESIGN MARGIN AND THERMAL NOTE (engineering judgment, not regulation)

250 psig is a legal minimum, not a design target. Propane vapor pressure is strongly temperature-dependent (approximate values, verify against a current table before use in calculations): ~92 psig at 60 F, ~172 psig at 100 F, ~225 psig at 120 F, ~250 psig at 130 F, ~290 psig at 140 F. A 250 psig-rated component sitting in a hot enclosure or on a sun-exposed skid is therefore at or above its rating at plausible summer skin temperatures, independent of any system fault.

Recommendation: specify components at >= 350 psig rated working pressure (or at the container's relief-device set pressure, whichever is higher) rather than the 250 psig floor, and pressure-derate non-metallic seals for the maximum expected ambient. Where the container relief device is set above 250 psig, components between the container and the first stage of regulation can see that higher pressure; sizing them to 250 psig only is technically compliant with (7)(i) but leaves no margin against the relief setting. Typical proof-test practice for the selected components is 1.5x rated (375 psig for a 250 psig part), which also gives a clean incoming-inspection criterion; note that 1.5x is a component-standard practice, whereas the section itself only requires leak-testing assembled piping at not less than normal operating pressure.


7. ASSUMPTIONS AND HOW TO RE-VERIFY

- Assumed: the requester wants the numeric rating from the regulation's own text, in psi(g), which is the unit the regulation uses ('p.s.i.g.'). 250 psig = 1.72 MPa gauge if SI is needed.
- Assumed: 'as in force on 2026-11-21' means the section text effective that date, with no pending amendments treated as effective early.
- Re-verification procedure: open eCFR Title 29 > Subtitle B > Chapter XVII > Part 1910 > Subpart H > 1910.110; use the 'Published Edition / Current' date selector set to a date on or before 2026-11-21; search the page for '250 p.s.i.g.' and read subparagraphs (7)(i) and (5)(i)/(5)(vi); cross-check against the GPO annual edition for the corresponding year. Confirm the 'authority' and 'source' lines at the bottom of the section to fix the amendment date, and check the Federal Register history for any document affecting 1910.110 between the annual edition and 2026-11-21.

verdict.summary:
# Maximum permitted start-to-discharge pressure setting - LP-Gas hydrostatic relief valve between shut-off valves

## Answer

**500 psig** (gauge). The limit is an inclusive ceiling: a valve whose marked start-to-discharge pressure is exactly 500 psig complies; anything above 500 psig does not.

Metric equivalent for reference only (do not use for valve marking): 500 psig = 3.45 MPa gauge = 3.55 MPa absolute.

## Governing provision

**29 CFR 1910.110(b)(10)(xii)** - *Storage and handling of liquefied petroleum gases.* Verbatim (eCFR current text, fetched 2026-11-23):

> "(xii) A hydrostatic relief valve shall be installed between each pair of shut-off valves on liquefied petroleum gas liquid piping so as to relieve into a safe atmosphere. **The start-to-discharge pressure setting of such relief valves shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g.** The minimum setting on relief valves installed in piping connected to other than DOT containers shall not be lower than 140 percent of the container relief valve setting and in piping connected to DOT containers not lower than 400 p.s.i.g. The start-to-discharge pressure setting of such a relief valve, if installed on the discharge side of a pump, shall be greater than the maximum pressure permitted by the recirculation device in the system."

The liquid-piping subparagraph of 1910.110 cross-references this same clause verbatim: *"(4) Hydrostatic relief valves shall be installed in accordance with paragraph (b)(10)(xii) of this section."* So there is one governing provision, not a set of competing ones.

## Currency verification for the 2026-11-21 'as in force' date

The figure is not date-sensitive across any edition in the record:

| Source | Edition / fetch date | Text of the setting limit |
|---|---|---|
| eCFR 'current' (title 29, subpart H, 1910.110) | fetched 2026-11-23 | "shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g." |
| GovInfo CFR 2025, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910.110 (PDF) | 2025 annual edition | "shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g." |
| GovInfo CFR 2025, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910.110 (XML) | 2025 annual edition | "shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g." |
| GovInfo CFR 2021, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910.110 (PDF) | 2021 annual edition | "shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g." |

Identical wording in the 2021 edition, the 2025 annual edition (the edition in force on 2026-11-21 absent an interim amendment), and the live eCFR text fetched two days after that date. No amendment affecting the 500 psig figure exists in the record. The answer is therefore the same whether read from the annual edition covering 2026-11-21 or from current eCFR.

## Units and notation

The regulation states the limit in **p.s.i.g. - gauge pressure**. Do not restate the set point in psia when marking, tagging, or specifying the valve. (500 psig = 514.7 psia at standard atmosphere; the 14.7 psi offset is larger than most relief-valve setting tolerances and is a classic field error.)

## Setting window - all constraints acting on this valve

| Constraint | Direction | Value | Clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Absolute ceiling on start-to-discharge setting | setting <= | **500 psig** | (b)(10)(xii) |
| Floor, piping connected to **DOT** containers | setting >= | 400 psig | (b)(10)(xii) |
| Floor, piping connected to **non-DOT** containers | setting >= | 1.40 x (container relief valve setting) | (b)(10)(xii) |
| Pump discharge side | setting > | maximum pressure permitted by the system recirculation device | (b)(10)(xii) |
| Placement | - | one valve between **each pair** of shut-off valves on LP-Gas liquid piping | (b)(10)(xii) |
| Discharge | - | must relieve **into a safe atmosphere** | (b)(10)(xii) |

Only the first row is a maximum. The 400 psig and 140% figures are **minimums** and do not change the ceiling; the DOT/non-DOT distinction affects only the floor, never the cap.

## Selection procedure

1. Identify the container type served by the liquid line: DOT (portable/transport) or non-DOT (ASME stationary).
2. Establish the container relief-valve set pressure, Pc, from the container's nameplate/ASME data and the applicable 1910.110(b)(10) table for that container type.
3. Compute the floor:
   - DOT-connected piping: F = 400 psig.
   - Non-DOT-connected piping: F = 1.40 x Pc.
4. If the valve sits on the **discharge side of a pump**, also determine the maximum pressure the system's recirculation (bypass) device permits, Pr, and set a pump-side floor Fp = Pr + a positive margin (the rule says only "greater than"; a practical margin of at least 5% or 10 psi is normal to stay clear of set-point tolerance and chatter).
5. Required minimum setting F_req = max(F, Fp) as applicable.
6. Select a hydrostatic relief valve whose **marked** start-to-discharge pressure satisfies F_req <= setting <= **500 psig**.
7. Verify the discharge is piped/positioned to a safe atmosphere and that the valve is installed between the shut-off valve pair, not on only one side of it.

### Conflict case (must be recognized, not designed around)

If step 3 or 4 yields F_req > 500 psig - e.g. non-DOT piping where 1.40 x Pc exceeds 500 psig, or a pump recirculation setting near the cap - **no single valve setting satisfies both the floor and the ceiling**, and the 500 psig ceiling in (b)(10)(xii) cannot be exceeded or waived. The resolution is upstream of the relief valve: lower the container relief-valve setting or the pump recirculation/bypass set point until the floor falls at or below 500 psig. Selecting a valve marked above 500 psig to satisfy the floor is a violation of the ceiling and is not an acceptable engineering resolution.

## Scope notes / common misapplications

- **Device identity:** this is a *hydrostatic* relief valve protecting a liquid-filled pipe section trapped between two shut-off valves against thermal expansion - not a container safety-relief valve. Container relief valves are governed by the separate provisions of (b)(10) (installation on the vapor space, rate-of-discharge tables, discharge-header sizing, rain caps).
- **Different device, different number:** the hydrostatic relief valve required on the *vaporizer section of vaporizer-burners* has its own rule with a **minimum** of 250 psig ("shall be such as to protect the components involved, but not less than 250 p.s.i.g."). That is a different device and does not set or relax the 500 psig cap for between-shut-off-valve liquid piping.
- **Parameters not asked and not implied by 500 psig:** reseating pressure, relieving capacity, orifice size, and nameplate marking are separate requirements. Compliance with the 500 psig ceiling says nothing about whether the valve has adequate capacity for the trapped liquid volume.
- **As in force on 2026-11-21:** no edition or amendment in the record alters the figure; 500 psig is the correct value for that date.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

20 percent. Under 29 CFR 1910.179(h)(2)(i), the rated load divided by the number of parts of rope shall not exceed 20 percent of the nominal breaking strength of the rope. Expressed as a design factor, that is a minimum of 5.0 (5:1) on nominal breaking strength per rope part. The 20 percent is a ceiling, not a target.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

29 CFR 1910.179(h) Hoisting equipment — (2) Ropes — (i):

  "In using hoisting ropes, the crane manufacturer's recommendation shall be followed. The rated load divided by the number of parts of rope shall not exceed 20 percent of the nominal breaking strength of the rope."

Three operative elements, in order of precedence as written:
  (a) The crane manufacturer's recommendation governs use of the hoisting rope. The 20 percent figure is the regulatory floor/backstop, not a substitute for the manufacturer's rope specification.
  (b) The quantity regulated is (rated load) / (number of parts of rope) — i.e., the nominal tension per rope part, not the total load and not the actual measured tension.
  (c) That per-part quantity may not exceed 20 percent of the rope's nominal breaking strength.

2. DATE-OF-FORCE VERIFICATION (discharges the constraint in ask 1)

  - eCFR current text, 29 CFR 1910.179, fetched 2026-11-23T10:53:45Z (sha256 3eb1ac03cbe8): contains the 20 percent sentence verbatim at (h)(2)(i).
  - GovInfo, CFR-2025 title 29 vol. 5, §1910.179 (7-1-25 edition), page 574: contains the 20 percent sentence verbatim at (h)(2)(i).
  - GovInfo, CFR-2011 title 29 vol. 5, §1910.179: contains the same 20 percent sentence verbatim at (h)(2)(i).

Conclusion: the figure has been 20 percent across the 2011 and 2025 print editions and in the eCFR text current as of the fetch two days after the as-of date. No amendment in that span changed the number. Residual caveat: the eCFR snapshot is dated 2026-11-23, not 2026-11-21; a Federal Register amendment effective exactly 2026-11-21 or 2026-11-22 that was itself superseded within two days would not be visible. Given the provision is unchanged across at least 14 years of print editions, this is a documentary caveat, not a substantive uncertainty.

3. DEFINITIONAL NOTES AFFECTING APPLICATION

  - "Rated load" is defined at §1910.179(b)(50) as "the maximum load for which a crane or individual hoist is designed and built by the manufacturer and shown on the equipment nameplate(s)." Use the nameplate value, not an informally estimated load and not the weight of the load alone where the standard's "load" definition (§1910.179(b)(45): total superimposed weight on the load block or hook) applies elsewhere in the section.
  - "Number of parts of rope" is the number of rope lines supporting the load block (the reeving count), not the number of falls on the drum.
  - "Nominal breaking strength" is the rope's catalog/nominal breaking strength, i.e., the published strength of the rope construction and diameter. It is not the same convention as a minimum breaking force (MBF) calculated to a standard such as ISO 2408 or a specific ASME/API rope specification. Where the manufacturer publishes both a nominal breaking strength and an MBF, the regulation's words point at the nominal figure; if only an MBF is available, using it is conservative (MBF <= nominal), so the 20 percent check remains satisfied. This convention gap should be stated on any calculation sheet rather than silently substituted.
  - Scope: (h)(2)(i) governs hoisting ropes. 1910.179 contains no separate percentage-of-breaking-strength limit for other rope uses; sling and below-the-hook rigging is outside 1910.179 (see 1910.184 for slings).
  - ASME B30 series standards are incorporated by reference into 1910.179 for crane construction, but the 20 percent figure is stated on the face of 1910.179(h)(2)(i) and is not displaced by them. A manufacturer's recommendation more restrictive than 20 percent controls per the first sentence of (h)(2)(i).

4. WORKED VERIFICATION (shows the number is self-consistent)

  Rope: nominal breaking strength NBS = 100 kN (illustrative). Reeving: n = 4 parts.
  Allowable per-part tension = 0.20 x NBS = 20.0 kN.
  Maximum rated load = 20.0 kN x 4 = 80.0 kN.
  Check: rated load / parts = 80.0 / 4 = 20.0 kN = 20.0 percent of NBS. Design factor = 100 / 20 = 5.0.
  The computed per-part utilization equals the 20 percent ceiling exactly; it does not exceed it. Any design that pushes rated load above 80 kN in this configuration violates 1910.179(h)(2)(i).

  Inverse form for field use: minimum required nominal breaking strength = 5 x (rated load / number of parts of rope).

5. PRACTICAL APPLICATION RULE

  For each hoisting rope reeving: compute (nameplate rated load) / (number of parts of rope); divide by the rope's nominal breaking strength; the result must be <= 0.20. Equivalently, require NBS >= 5 x rated load / parts. Where the crane manufacturer specifies a heavier rope or a higher design factor, the manufacturer's recommendation controls.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1910.180(d)(2)(ii), the periodic inspection interval stated for crawler, locomotive, and truck cranes is a range: 1 to 12 months, unless the manufacturer specifically recommends otherwise.

Verbatim text of the governing provision (§ 1910.180(d)(2), 'Regular inspection'):

  '(2) Regular inspection. Inspection procedure for cranes in regular service is divided into two general classifications based upon the intervals at which inspection should be performed. The intervals in turn are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. The two general classifications are herein designated as "frequent" and "periodic", with respective intervals between inspections as defined below:
   (i) Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals.
   (ii) Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.'

CITATION AND READING

- Cite as: 29 CFR § 1910.180(d)(2)(ii) (Crawler locomotive and truck cranes — Inspection classification — Regular inspection — Periodic inspection).
- The paragraph lettering is confirmed internally: § 1910.180(d)(3) directs that frequent-inspection items be inspected 'at intervals as defined in paragraph (d)(2)(i) of this section', which places 'Frequent inspection' at (d)(2)(i) and 'Periodic inspection' at (d)(2)(ii).
- 1 to 12 months is a range, not a fixed period. The employer sets the actual interval within that range based on the criticality of the components and their degree of exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. 12 months is the outer bound — the longest default interval the standard permits. A 12-month program satisfies the text only where the exposure analysis supports it; the standard does not authorize exceeding 12 months absent a manufacturer's specific recommendation.
- The manufacturer caveat is part of the same sentence ('or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer'). A manufacturer's specific recommendation displaces the 1-to-12-month default for the affected components/model; a generic or non-specific recommendation does not. Where the manufacturer recommends a shorter interval, follow the shorter interval; where it recommends a longer one, the manufacturer's specific recommendation controls under the text of (d)(2)(ii), but document the basis (make, model, manual section, date) in the inspection program file.

SCOPE — DOES IT APPLY UNIFORMLY TO ALL THREE CRANE TYPES?

Yes. Section 1910.180(b)(1) (Application) reaches 'crawler cranes, locomotive cranes, wheel mounted cranes of both truck and self-propelled wheel type, and any variations thereof which retain the same fundamental characteristics.' The definitions of crawler, locomotive, and truck crane are at § 1910.180(a)(1)-(3). Paragraph (d)(2) states a single inspection classification scheme for 'cranes in regular service' and does not differentiate the periodic interval by crane type. The 1-to-12-month periodic interval therefore applies alike to crawler, locomotive, and truck cranes.

DISTINCTIONS THE READER MUST NOT CONFLATE

- Frequent inspection, § 1910.180(d)(2)(i): daily to monthly. This is a separate, shorter-interval classification, not the periodic interval.
- Periodic inspection, § 1910.180(d)(2)(ii): 1 to 12 months, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer. This is the answer.
- Initial inspection, § 1910.180(d)(1): before initial use of all new and altered cranes — not an interval.
- Running-rope inspection, § 1910.180(g)(1): 'A thorough inspection of all ropes in use shall be made at least once a month.' This is an independent, separately cited requirement; it does not modify (d)(2)(ii) and does not convert the periodic interval into a monthly requirement.
- The itemized list of what a periodic inspection must cover is in the paragraphs following (d)(3); it is not reproduced here because the exact verbatim text of that list was not among the verified passages, and it does not affect the interval answer.

CURRENCY VERIFICATION FOR THE 2026-11-21 DATE

The quoted sentence was confirmed identical in four independently published renderings:
1. eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.180 (current), fetched 2026-11-23T10:56:29Z, sha256 4b691b428b80 — two days after the target date, so the text bracketing 2026-11-21 is the same text.
2. GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 29 vol. 5, § 1910.180 (edition date 2025-07-01), fetched 2026-11-23T10:56:29Z, sha256 d9085ead045f.
3. A printed 7-1-09 edition rendering (§ 1910.180(d)(2)(ii)), fetched 2026-11-23T10:56:30Z, sha256 1d9049fb30c4.
4. GovInfo, CFR 2004 title 29 vol. 5, § 1910.180, fetched 2026-11-23T10:56:29Z, sha256 597e77ff9ea1.
The only amendment noted in the fetched material is an editorial nomenclature change at 84 FR 21597 (May 14, 2019), which does not touch (d)(2)(ii). Because the operative sentence is unchanged from the 2004 edition through the 2025 edition and through the eCFR snapshot taken after the target date, no amendment affecting the periodic inspection interval had taken effect as of 2026-11-21 in the sources reviewed.

HOW TO APPLY (inspection-program procedure)

1. Classify each crane as crawler, locomotive, or truck per § 1910.180(a)(1)-(3); confirm it is in scope under (b)(1).
2. Establish a documented periodic inspection interval within 1 to 12 months, justified by component criticality and exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction (d)(2).
3. Check the manufacturer's manual for that make/model. If it states a specific inspection interval, adopt that interval in place of the default and record the manual citation (make, model, manual revision, section, date) in the program file.
4. Keep the periodic (complete) inspection record separate from frequent-inspection records and from the monthly running-rope inspection required by (g)(1).
5. Re-verify the regulatory text against eCFR before relying on this answer for any date other than 2026-11-21.
